the detection of DNA adducts in the cells of the respiratory system of individuals exposed to carcinogenic compounds.
the study of the relationship between the internal exposure to benzo[a] pyrene and the risk of lung cancer, a major health problem in the developed countries.
the development of new methods for the detection and quantitation of DNA adducts, with a view to their application in molecular epidemiology studies of cancer.

the detection of BPDE DNA adducts in the cells recovered from bronchoalveoloal lavage is a useful biomonitoring tool in molecular epidemiological studies.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we were able to demonstrate the formation of DNA adducts in the alveolar macrophas of smokers.

we have demonstrated that benzo[a] pyrene diolepoxide DNA adducts can be detected in alveolar cells of smokers and ex-smokers, and that the amount of DNA adducts is related to the number of cigarettes smoked per day.
the detection of benzo[a]-pyrene diolepoxides in alveolar cells is a good indicator of the internal dose of the carcinogen.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of BPDE-DN adducts in cells of the lung is associated with the number of smoked cigarettes, and the number of cigarettes smoked in the last 6 month.
it is possible to detect DNA adducts in the lungs of smokers and former smokers, which is an important finding because DNA adducts are the ultimate cause of lung cancer.
the use of bronchoalveoloar lavage to collect cells for analysis of DNA adducts is a sensitive and specific tool, which can be used to monitor exposure to carcinogens.
